slides.text:
`match` compares one value with a list of patterns, from the top, and runs the first arm that fits. Here the patterns are plain values and `_`.

The snippet is pseudo code, not Rust.

You will use `match` as a statement and as an expression that gives a value, on integers, bools and chars.

Ranges, several patterns in one arm and conditions on an arm are taught in `literal-and-range-patterns`. Enums come later too.

Each arm is `pattern => code`. The arms are tried from the top, the first that fits runs and the rest are skipped.

`_` fits any value, so it goes last to catch what the other arms did not.

slides.text:
A `match` must cover every possible value, or the program does not compile.

A bool has two values, so `true` and `false` are enough. An integer has far too many to list, so a match on one ends with `_`.

chunks.guide: A command and a starting position.
Char patterns are char literals in single quotes. Each arm changes the position, and the catch-all reports a letter it does not know.

notes.text: A char pattern is a char literal in single quotes.
The arm runs this statement when the command is 'd'.

chunks.text:
match command {
        'u' => row -= 1,
        'd' => row += 1,
        'l' => col -= 1,
        'r' => col += 1,
        _ => println!("unknown command"),
    }

chunks.guide: Print the new position.
